It looks at how accountability is shared among system designers, vendors, deployers, and human operators when AI-driven tools are used to influence detection actions, prioritization, and response. The chapter investigates legal principles explaining the relationship between control, foreseeability, and duty of care, along with regulatory requirements for human oversight and governance. It also examines issues related to automation bias, black-box models, and extended decision chains that involve Security Operations Centers and third parties. Special focus is given to documentation, role clarity, chain of command for escalation, and auditability as means of defining responsibility. Through combining a legal perspective with security operational practice, the chapter outlines a system for determining responsibility, handling liability, and making defensible decisions in AI-assisted security systems.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4018/979-8-2600-2870-4.ch007\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 7, 9]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.66695/ijir.v1i1.009\", \"title\": [\"Algorithmic Decision-Making Systems and Legal Responsibility: Reconstructing Fault, Agency, and Accountability in the Digital Age\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Abstract In the digital age, algorithmic decision-making systems have become central actors in shaping legal, econo…
